column2: In 1914, the South Pole had already been reached. Roald Amundsen got there first in 1911.
So Ernest Shackleton chose a bigger goal. To walk across the whole of Antarctica, from one sea to the other.
The plan was to land on the coast of the Weddell Sea, march to the South Pole, and carry on to the Ross Sea. About 2,900 kilometres on foot.
His ship was called Endurance. A three-masted wooden ship, built to push through ice.
On board were twenty-seven men chosen by Shackleton. And one he had turned down.
Perce Blackborow, nineteen years old, had stowed away. Shackleton was furious. He told him that if they ran out of food, he would be the first one eaten.
Then he signed him on as a steward. The crew was now twenty-eight.
In November 1914, Endurance reached South Georgia, a whaling island in the South Atlantic. The last human settlement on their route.
The whalers there gave a warning. The ice in the Weddell Sea was worse that year than anyone could remember.
Shackleton waited a month. Then, on the fifth of December 1914, he sailed anyway.
